According to recent reports, puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

Industry observers note that the opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

In a recent development, puppies learn quickly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

All puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Sources indicate that obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and newly introduced situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

Recent findings suggest that most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health challenges is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

It has been revealed that puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

According to recent reports, most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

Activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

In a recent development, most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

Sources indicate that A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

Traditions connect generations, carrying the cultural and moral values of ancestors to newly introduced generations, giving them a sense of identity and belonging. Some of these traditions are so lovely that they are adopted more widely. The beautiful old Christmas tradition of Christmas wheat is one of them.

Recent findings suggest that the sowing of Christmas wheat is a tradition across Europe from France to Ukraine and the Balkans. Early in December, people “plant” wheatgrass seeds in bowls indoors early in December and let the shoots grow until Christmas. Initially the growing wheat seeds were considered a blessing for the coming harvest. But beyond that, the green shoots have come to symbolize fertility, newly introduced life, and eternal renewal.

You don’t have to live in the South of France or other parts of Europe to practice this lovely tradition. We’ll tell you all about the custom of growing wheatgrass indoors and how you can make it your own this Christmas.

All around the globe, cultural heritage shapes how people celebrate, and also how they express beauty. The lovely tradition of planting Christmas wheat is still very much a part of Christmas festivities in Europe, thought to have been inherited from the Romans.

It is practiced in the Province area of France, as well as Croatia, Ukraine, and parts of Italy and Portugal, each region claiming it as their own. In Province, it is called Saint-Barbe wheat (le blé de la Sainte-Barbe) because the day of planting, December 4, is the feast day of Saint Barbara. By Christmas day, the seeds have grown fresh green shoots that become decorations on the Christmas table.

In Province, this age-old tradition involves sprouting grains of wheat in three separate bowls. The ritual is stated to ensure prosperity and happiness for the coming year, a promise memorialized in the old Provençal adage, “when wheat goes well, everything goes well.”.

In Croatia, the origins of this tradition are still related to religion, but they are different. Growing wheatgrass is related to the story of the holy family fleeing Herod’s soldiers. It is stated that the family found a farmer sowing wheat. The family requested that the farmer tell the Herod’s soldiers that the family had already passed through.

The wheat grew remarkably fast that year so by the time the soldiers came, there was a fine crop. Then, the farmer told them that the family passed through while he was sowing his crop. Because the wheat was so tall, the soldiers assumed that the family had passed by long ago and abandoned their quest. As such, wheat seeds are sown in December to represent light found amid the winter's darkness.

So, how to grow your own wheat?

Well, if you would like to incorporate this ancient tradition into your own holiday celebrations, we’ll walk you through the steps. There are three: gather what you need, “plant” the seeds, then arrange the centerpiece.

Sources indicate that the most important "ingredient" you will require to grow your own Christmas wheat are the wheat grains themselves. Traditionally, you use hard red winter wheat berries (sold as "wheatgrass seeds”) although it is possible to use alternatives like lentils or chickpeas instead.

According to recent reports, the presentation also varies from region to region. In Province, for Saint Barbe’s wheat, they use three small bowls or saucers and damp cotton wool. The three containers have religious significance, representing the Holy Trinity. In Croatia, you can use any container, but you still need to line it with either cotton wool or soil as a growing medium. A more practical alternative is to use a growing tray filled with potting soil with a solid tray beneath it to catch water.

Industry observers note that soak the grains overnight in water. After that, place them evenly on the growing medium - like the bed of damp cotton wool or the potting soil. If you are using three bowls, spread it evenly between them. If you are using a tray, spread the seeds there.

Recent findings suggest that place the seeded container near a bright window at a mild temperature. Spray it with water and cover with plastic paper or a plastic bag. Remove this plastic when the seeds begin to germinate.

In a recent development, mist the cotton with water daily to keep it moist. This allows the shoots to germinate and grow straight and green.

Recent findings suggest that how you choose to arrange the centerpiece depends entirely on your own preferences and traditions. By Christmas Eve, the little shoots are green and straight,.

It has been revealed that in Croatia, the wheat sprouts are often decorated with the Croatian tricolour – a red-white-blue ribbon. This adds patriotic symbolism. The Croatians sometimes add a red candle or even a red apple in the centre of the container to add more holiday cheer.

According to recent reports, in Province, the French often toe up the sprouted wheat with red and yellow or red and green ribbons. The wheat display becomes the centerpiece for their traditional Christmas Eve feast. After Christmas, the French place the pots in or near the family crèche (aka the nativity scene) alongside handmade clay saint images. Finally, the wheat can be planted in open ground or burned in the fireplace for protection.

Recent findings suggest that remember, this is a lovely tradition, but while wheatgrass might look like a microgreen it should not be used as one. Yes, it has many incredible health properties (it is noted to prevent some types of cancer, fight infection and improve cognitive function), but it is not edible.

That being mentioned, you can juice it and drink its juice, which is full of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Sounds like a great tipple after a massive holiday feast, eh?

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, Upcoming York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

Industry observers note that chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

It has been revealed that chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Sources indicate that chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, swiftly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

It has been revealed that chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

Sources indicate that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

How to Winterize Your Lawn Mower – 6 Easy Steps to Keep It Running Smoothly Next Spring

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year.

  • I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year. All you want to do is push that lawn mower into the shed and close and lock the door. But you can’t, and you’ll regret it if you do. Come the following spring, you’ll pull out a mower that is sluggish, with stale fuel, clogged carburetors, and broken parts. It’s entirely possible that that lawn mower won’t start in spring at all.

You can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance. It’s not as nice as tucking that mower away and drinking a cool beer, but it’s not all that difficult either. Once you learn how to winterize a lawn mower, you’ll find that it’s easier to jump in and do the work before you move your machine into winter storage.

I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest. Just follow this practical step-by-step approach. It won't take long if you tackle it alongside your other garden winterizing chores.

Sources indicate that it only takes a month for the gasoline in a gas-powered motor to start to break down. When it does, it leaves gummy deposits in the carburetor. This doesn’t do anything good for the mower. You can tackle this in either of two ways.

It has been revealed that first, and some would argue best, is to add a lawn mower fuel stabilizer to the remaining fresh gasoline in the tank. Sta-Bil, available on Amazon, is a good choice, but Sea Foam and Ethanol Shield are other popular options. But check your mower manufacturer's recommendations, as some don't advise this step.

According to recent reports, to use a fuel stabilizer, first check the product instructions for the correct amount to add based on the gasoline volume. Add the stabilizer to the tank, then top up with fresh gasoline, leaving a little room for expansion. Run the engine for around 5-10 minutes, or as directed on the product label, to allow the treated fuel to circulate through the fuel system. This helps prevent gasoline from deteriorating during winter storage, reducing the risk of deposits forming in the carburetor and causing starting problems in spring.

The second option to winterize a gas mower is to empty the tank so that there is no gasoline to break down. You can do this easily by running the mower until it is totally out of gas. You can also empty the tank by draining the tank and carburetor bowl manually.

In a recent development, before you start, switch off the engine, let it cool completely, and disconnect the spark plug wire for safety. If you need to tip the mower to access the underside, tilt it with the air filter and carburetor facing upward, as tipping it the wrong way can allow oil or fuel to leak into the air filter or engine intake.

Sources indicate that next, clean the underside of the mower, scraping away grass clippings and dirt with a plastic scraper or stiff nylon brush. Leaving damp debris in place over winter can cause corrosion on steel mower decks.

Recent findings suggest that once the underside is clean and completely dry, apply a protective coating. Mo-Deck Non-Stick Mower Deck Spray helps prevent grass clippings and debris from sticking to the deck, making cleanup easier when mowing season returns. Follow the product instructions and allow it to dry before storing the mower.

Sources indicate that draining the oil is not fun, but it’s not that difficult either. First, check your mower's manual, as some newer engines only require oil top-ups rather than regular changes. If yours needs an oil change, run the mower for a few minutes to warm the oil, then switch off the engine, let it cool enough to work safely, and disconnect the spark plug wire before proceeding.

Drain the old, dirty oil into a suitable container, following your mower's instructions. A Briggs & Stratton oil extractor kit makes the job much less messy, allowing you to remove oil through the fill tube without tipping the mower.

In a recent development, does your mower have an oil filter? If so, change it now, using a replacement designed for your engine. Then refill with the correct amount of fresh motor oil. This will depend on your model, but common options include SAE 30 and synthetic 5W-30. Check the oil level with the dipstick to avoid overfilling, and take the used oil to a recycling facility.

Your lawn mower blade needs to be sharp and free of cracks. With the engine off and the spark plug wire disconnected, follow your mower's instructions to safely access and remove the blade. Wear thick gloves and check carefully for nicks, cracks, bends, or dull edges.

Sources indicate that you can sharpen a dull blade with a hand file, but it's easier to use a proper lawn mower blade sharpener, like this Sporgain lawn mower blade sharpener and balancer from Amazon. However, if your lawn mower blade is cracked or badly damaged, it's better to replace it.

If you sharpen the blade yourself, follow the manufacturer's recommended angle and make sure it's properly balanced before reinstalling it. An unbalanced blade can cause excessive vibration and damage the mower.

Sources indicate that at the same time, inspect the spark plug for wear, corrosion, or heavy carbon buildup. Remove it using a spark plug socket (this Milwaukee set from Home Depot has three sizes), and if the plug is damaged, badly worn, or heavily coated, it's best to replace it with a newly introduced one recommended for your mower. Otherwise, gently clean away any light buildup with a soft brush before putting it back. Check your mower's manual for any specific instructions.

According to recent reports, the great thing about winterizing a battery-operated mower is that you don’t have to worry about gasoline problems. On the other hand, you do have to worry about looking after the battery. This is also important if your gasoline-powered mower has an electric starter.

Proper winter storage is essential. If the battery is removable, take it out of the mower and store it in a cool, dry place indoors, away from freezing temperatures and extreme heat. Check your manufacturer's recommendations for the ideal storage temperature, as requirements vary between batteries.

For lithium-ion batteries, most manufacturers recommend storing them partially charged, rather than fully charged or empty. Check the charge periodically throughout winter and top it up if needed.

In a recent development, however, if your mower uses a lead-acid battery, you generally need to keep it fully charged during storage. A compatible battery maintainer can help prevent them from going flat. The Noco Genius1 Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer maintains the battery's charge throughout winter so it's ready to go when mowing season returns. Do make sure any charger or maintainer you use is suitable for your battery type.

According to recent reports, move your mower into a dry shed, garage, or other sheltered space where it will be protected from rain, snow, and ice. Ideally, keep it on a clean, dry surface, as sitting on damp ground over winter can cause rust and corrosion.

According to recent reports, A breathable, water-resistant lawn mower cover, like this Himal Outdoors Push Lawn Mower Cover from Amazon, is a good idea because it helps keep dust, dirt, and moisture off the mower when it's not in use. Make sure the mower is completely cool and dry before covering it.

According to recent reports, avoid storing your mower near corrosive household chemicals, fertilizers, or pool chlorine, as their fumes or spills can damage metal components over time. If you're storing it in a garage or shed, leave enough space around the machine for ventilation and easy access.

Sources indicate that for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

What began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell rapidly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

By November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the company.

Sources indicate that the questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

In a recent development, different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

Biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

Sources indicate that exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Recent findings suggest that not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

Industry observers note that pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

Sources indicate that the scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

Sources indicate that the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) notes the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

Industry observers note that the death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

It has been revealed that people entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

Industry observers note that letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

Industry observers note that turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

According to recent reports, plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

According to recent reports, sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

Corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

According to recent reports, plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

Cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

Onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

Sources indicate that stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively swiftly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

It has been revealed that yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

It has been revealed that A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

Recent findings suggest that A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

According to recent reports, when it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

According to recent reports, thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

Industry observers note that the Korean War is often called Americaâs Forgotten War, with the dogs who served in it forgotten right along with it. Yet one platoon, and one dog in particular, quietly reshaped how the military would think about scout dogs for the rest of the twentieth century.

When North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, the United States military had almost nothing left of the war dog program that had served so effectively in World War II. After 1945, the Army had gutted its dog units, and only one platoon, the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon (26th ISDP), based first at Fort Riley, Kansas, survived intact. Before the war, this platoonâs main job was public demonstrations that showcased military dog capabilities to American audiences.

Scout dogs in Korea were not attack dogs in the way many people imagine war dogs to be. Their central task was to give a silent alert, typically by freezing, raising their hackles, or pointing, when they detected enemy soldiers ahead of a patrol, at an observation post, or forward of the front lines. Nearly all of these patrols took place at night, when human senses were least reliable, and the risk of walking into an ambush was highest.

According to recent reports, over the course of the war, the 26th ISDP conducted more than 1,500 combat patrols. A Review of after-action reports credited scout dog teams with reducing casualty rates among the patrols they accompanied by 65 percent, an extraordinary figure for a single battlefield innovation.

The dogs became well known, even feared, on the other side of the line, too. Historical accounts describe Chinese forces using loudspeakers along the front to broadcast messages to American troops that reportedly included the line, âYankee, take your dog and go home!â.

According to recent reports, among the dogs of the 26th ISDP, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record: Scout Dog York, service number 011X. York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

Industry observers note that other dogs in the platoon earned similar renown. Arlo, another German Shepherd, is remembered for helping his patrol avoid what is believed to have been a near-certain ambush. Handler accounts and unit histories also mention dogs named Happy, Champ, and Hasso as part of the platoonâs roster of effective scout teams during the conflict.

The 26th ISDP served in Korea from June 1951 until the July 1953 armistice. Over that time, its members, both human and canine alike, were awarded a total of three Silver Stars, six Bronze Stars for Valor, and thirty-five Bronze Stars for Meritorious Service. On February 27, 1953, the Department of the Army formally recognized the platoonâs accomplishments in General Order No. 21.

Unlike the individual medal controversies that followed Chips during WWII, official recognition of the Korean War scout dogs came largely through unit citations rather than personal decorations for the animals themselves, an approach that seems to have avoided the same public dispute over honoring dogs with human military awards.

Industry observers note that before the Korean War, the scout dog program had all but disappeared. In 1946, the Armyâs Committee on Organization at Fort Benning debated whether to keep infantry war dog platoons active. Committee chairman Brigadier General Frederick McCabe recommended retaining them and attaching them to infantry training units; a recommendation that was largely ignored. Instead, the Quartermaster Corps shifted toward purchasing dogs directly from breeders rather than sustaining a broader loan program with the public. Had the 26th ISDP not survived this postwar contraction, the United States might have entered Korea with no scout dog capability at all.

Recent findings suggest that the success of the 26th ISDP in Korea, epitomized by dogs like York, helped ensure scout dogs would never again be allowed to disappear from the Armyâs order of battle as they had after 1945. When American forces deployed to Vietnam a little more than a decade later, the Army reactivated its scout dog program in 1965, drawing directly on lessons learned in Korea.

Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds.
  • The mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth.
  • Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds. They're the backbone of a winter garden, which is why it's so disappointing to find brown or black leaf tips on a hebe, photinia, choisya, arborvitae or other evergreens after the first cold snap. And this year, evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips are a problem many gardeners are facing as temperatures drop.

The mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

Blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is notable so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:.

Industry observers note that if the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

Industry observers note that there are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

Recent findings suggest that your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

Sources indicate that during a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing newly introduced, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

In a recent development, some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

Desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

Industry observers note that distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from fresh foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the glitch, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

It has been revealed that evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

According to recent reports, first – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

Recent findings suggest that now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

If those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

Next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

According to recent reports, now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

These steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s crucial not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger fresh growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

Wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout new growth.

It has been revealed that keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:.

Dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic problem, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

Industry News: Mini Greenhouse or Cold Frame? Discover Which is Better to Protect Your Plants From Winter Weather

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is.
  • According to recent reports, A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover.
  • Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

According to recent reports, A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

Most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

Industry observers note that cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

Recent findings suggest that plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

In a recent development, so, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to swiftly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

When buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

When buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

It has been revealed that PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

Look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

Double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

Reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

It's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick substantial bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

Recent findings suggest that A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

In a recent development, if you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

In a recent development, whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

Tech Report: How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical.
  • In a recent development, all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues.
  • Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical. We've all been there: you choose one that looks promising at the lot, then get it home and discover it's too tall or wide for your living room – or simply looks much more awkwardly shaped than you remembered. It’s enough to make you open the bottle of sherry you left out for Santa.

In a recent development, all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues. But a little careful pruning can make a big difference. Here, we will explain the steps to trim a too-tall, too-wide, or lopsided Christmas tree into a balanced, attractive centerpiece. We’ll also lay out the tools you need and the techniques you should use.

Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place. Before you begin trimming, remember that removing branches is much easier than putting them back. Work gradually, and try repositioning or fluffing branches before reaching for your pruners.

A beautifully shaped Christmas tree should have a straight central trunk, a strong top branch to support a star or angel, and evenly spaced branches that create a full, balanced appearance.

Commercial Christmas tree growers tend to encourage the classic conical Christmas tree shape through occasional pruning. They aim for a base width of around 60 to 70 percent of the tree's height, although a slimmer tree may be more practical for smaller rooms.

Branch density matters, too. Large gaps between branch tiers can make a tree look sparse, while more closely spaced tiers create a fuller appearance – though denser branch tiers mean less space to hang ornaments.

The first step, once you bring the new tree into your home, is to make a fresh, straight cut about half an inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the trunk. Some sellers will do this for you before you load it into your car, but it needs to be fresh. If you're doing it yourself, a pruning saw, like Fiskars' Pro 10-Inch Pruning Saw, available on Amazon, will make the job easier. Then, put the tree straight into a sturdy container of water. This is one of the most important steps to make your Christmas tree last longer and prevent premature needle drop.

Let the tree settle before doing any further trimming. Give the tree a few hours, or ideally overnight, to relax its branches. This is particularly important if the tree has been tightly wrapped in netting. Its branches need time to spread back into their natural positions, and what initially looks like an awkward gap or uneven section may become much less noticeable.

In a recent development, once the branches have relaxed, walk around the tree and look at it from several angles. Identify any protruding branches, bare patches, or uneven growth before deciding what actually needs cutting.

You’ll need clean, sharp tools to prune a real Christmas tree into a pleasing cone shape. With the right tools and techniques, you can create a full, appealing tree no matter how tall, wide, or wonky it started out.

According to recent reports, you can buy a hundred different tools for pruning trees, but you really don’t need more than a handful to prune a real Christmas tree. For smaller branches, a pair of budget-friendly pruners, like Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, will give you the control needed to make clean, precise cuts. For thicker branches, use loppers, like Corona ComfortGEL Bypass Loppers, which provide extra cutting power.

Sources indicate that for cutting through the trunk, use a sharp pruning saw or handsaw. Make sure the cut is straight so the tree sits securely in its stand.

Recent findings suggest that is your Christmas tree too tall for your space? That’s usually one of the easiest Christmas tree problems to deal with, so don’t fret. First, measure your ceiling height, then subtract the height you need for the tree stand and tree topper, plus at least 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) of clearance. This is the perfect height for your new tree. Then measure the tree to see how much you need to remove.

If you only need a modest reduction (say, a few inches), cut the excess length from the bottom of the trunk. Just make sure enough bare trunk remains to fit securely into the stand without forcing the lower branches against its rim. Then put the tree into its stand – ideally one with a built-in water reservoir, like the Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand.

If your tree is significantly too tall, removing a large section of the trunk could also mean losing its attractive lower branches. In this case, you may need to shorten the central leader at the top instead. This is the upright shoot that forms the tree's tip.

Sometimes the leader is disproportionately tall and can easily be shortened without spoiling the tree's shape. Other times, cutting off the original tip can ruin its natural outline and remove the little knobbly buds and side shoots that help hold a tree topper in place. Indeed, it might be better to go without a topper rather than making a drastic cut. So treat trimming the tip of your Christmas tree as a last resort, and only if you think it will work with its natural shape.

If you do decide to take this step, trim the leader carefully to the desired height. Then assess the tree's fresh shape and, if necessary, selectively shorten the surrounding branches until you achieve a symmetrical, conical outline. Work gradually, stepping back regularly to check your progress.

In a recent development, when a tree is too wide to fit gracefully in your home, you can trim its branches. A traditionally shaped Christmas tree has a base width of around two-thirds its height. But it’s a good idea to measure the floor space where the tree will stand to make sure that the “ideal” shape will work for you.

Sources indicate that start by positioning the tree where you want it to stand and turning it to find the most attractive side. If branches at the back prevent it from fitting neatly against the wall, trim these first. Then, look at the tree from the front and sides, shortening any branches that stick out too far or spoil its overall shape.

According to recent reports, work gradually, removing a little at a time, and step back often to check the results. You don't need to trim every branch to the same length – the aim is to create a balanced, natural-looking tree that fits comfortably in its space.

For branches that genuinely need shortening, make cuts within the green, needle-covered portion of the growth. Avoid cutting too deeply into the bare, woody sections, as this can leave obvious gaps in the foliage that won't fill out.

Remember that different types of Christmas trees naturally have different shapes. Some firs have a dense, compact outline, while certain spruces and pines have more open branching. Work with the tree's natural form rather than trying to force every variety into exactly the same silhouette.

Sources indicate that it’s easier to talk about a too-tall or too-wide Christmas tree than one that’s just kind of weird. Whether it's lopsided or just plain wonky, you can still improve that uneven Christmas tree shape to make it presentable.

First, check that the trunk is standing straight in its base. Sometimes a tree that looks lopsided simply needs adjusting in the stand rather than pruning.

Recent findings suggest that to shape a lopsided Christmas tree, keep a cone shape in the front of your mind. Prune the upper branches shorter than the lower ones, and remember that the base width should be about two-thirds the tree's height. To achieve these goals, keep stepping back to see how things look.

It has been revealed that take off any dead or damaged branches, then clip back any that protrude too far and spoil the tree's outline. If one side is particularly dense, you can selectively shorten a few branches to create a more balanced appearance. Work gradually, as it's easy to remove too much.

It has been revealed that some unevenness comes from the way the tree grew. Christmas trees produce successive tiers of branches as they develop, and the amount of growth between these tiers influences how dense or open the finished tree appears. If one section has widely spaced branches, pruning alone won't necessarily make it look fuller.

Start by fluffing nearby branches or gently repositioning longer ones to disguise any gaps. You can also fold flexible branches into place and secure them with twine. If one side is woefully sparse, turn the tree so that this side is against the wall.

In a recent development, alternatively, you can borrow a branch from a particularly dense area of the tree and use it to fill an obvious gap. Simply cut the branch and secure it to the trunk or a sturdy neighboring branch with green wire, like this Pauleen floral wire from Amazon, positioning it to blend in with the surrounding foliage. Make sure it's firmly attached before adding any decorations.

If you'd rather not cut branches from elsewhere on your tree, artificial Christmas tree filler branches or greenery picks can work just as well. Look for ones that closely match the color and texture of your tree's needles, like these Hananona faux pine branches, and tuck them into sparse areas to create a fuller, more balanced appearance.

According to recent reports, you may also be able to disguise a sparse section by trimming back some of the heavier surrounding growth, helping the branches appear more evenly distributed. However, avoid cutting away too much greenery in an attempt to fill a gap – you could end up creating another one.

It has been revealed that the only time you have to worry about a tree’s health is when it is alive. If you have a cut Christmas tree, it is no longer growing. That means that you do not have to worry about its health. Instead, trim the tree to fit well and look nice in your home.

However, excessive Christmas tree shearing can still affect its appearance and stability. Removing too many lower branches may leave the trunk exposed, while cutting away large sections of the crown can make it difficult to achieve a natural shape.

Sources indicate that if, however, you buy a living Christmas tree you wish to plant, you do have to worry about keeping the tree healthy. Over-trimming can send the tree into shock or even kill it. The general rule is never to take off more than a quarter of the foliage annually. For most trimmings, stick to 10 percent.

Don't cut conifers back to the woody inner branches. Most will not sprout newly introduced needles from these branches. Limit your pruning to green, needle-bearing growth. The only exception is if you remove an entire branch back to the trunk.

If you're growing your own Christmas tree in the garden or keeping a living tree to use again in future years, pruning requires a different approach. Unlike a cut tree, a living evergreen needs to maintain healthy growth and develop a strong, balanced structure.

Young Christmas trees generally need only light corrective pruning during their first few years. This might involve removing damaged branches, correcting an uneven shape, or dealing with two competing upright shoots. Ideally, the tree should have one dominant central leader to maintain a straight trunk and a natural pointed crown.

Sources indicate that more regular shaping can begin as the tree becomes established, often around its third growing season. For many Christmas tree species, growers carry out their main shearing once the latest shoots have finished extending but before the fresh growth becomes fully firm. The timing varies according to the species and growing conditions.

It has been revealed that for a living Christmas tree you hope to keep for years, though, it's best to prune conservatively. Focus on correcting problems rather than heavily shearing the entire tree, and always check the pruning requirements of the particular species you're growing.

In a recent development, many people get overexcited when they start pruning a Christmas tree and are shocked to find out they have cut off too much. If this is you, take a breath. It’s only a Christmas tree. Resist the temptation to keep cutting elsewhere to even things up. A few strategically placed decorations will usually disguise the problem more effectively than further pruning.

If you have snipped a few times too many and created a bare spot (or two!), here are a few tips for covering up the damage:.

As you move through the necessary pruning, you’ll want to keep these few key rules in mind:.
