To find a selection of the best countertop water filters for home use, we began by evaluating dozens of popular models, focusing on ease of installation and use, filtration claims, capacity, and price.

It has been revealed that after selecting seven units for testing, we performed the same set of steps with each, starting with installation. Next, we performed water quality tests before and after filtration to measure contaminant reduction, followed by blind taste tests to rate flavor and odor. We measured flow rate by timing how long each unit took to process or dispense a quart of water, assessed how easy each unit was to clean and change filters on, and rated general convenience of extra features like filter life indicators and removable pitchers.

We used each model for a minimum of 2 days to get a feel for how much we liked them overall, and for the faucet-connected models, to see whether they got in the way during regular tasks like washing hands or dishes.

The best countertop water filtration system for your home will depend on the quality concerns you want to address, how much filtered water your household uses, and how much daily upkeep you’re willing to take on. It’s smart to request a copy of your local utility’s Consumer Confidence Report or use a home water test kit, then compare potential systems’ filtration claims, capacity, footprint, and replacement-filter cost.

Countertop water filters generally fall into two broad categories: reservoir-based systems and faucet-connected systems. Reservoir models don’t connect to your plumbing at all, while faucet-connected models attach to a standard faucet or use a diverter valve under your sink.

Reservoir systems hold untreated water in one tank or chamber and deliver clean water into another after it passes through the system’s filter(s). The simplest versions are water pitchers like the Epic Water Filters Pure XP Water Filter Pitcher or gravity systems like the Massive Berkey Gravity-Fed Water Filter. Since they don’t connect to your faucet, they’re great for apartments, dorms, RVs, and kitchens with incompatible faucets.

Countertop reverse osmosis systems also use a refillable reservoir, but rather than relying on gravity, they have an internal pump that forces the water through their filters before delivering it to a pitcher or your glass. RO systems have the added benefit of reducing dissolved solids in untreated water, but that includes beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium and also creates wastewater that must be dumped (or used for things like cleaning or watering plants).

It has been revealed that faucet-connected filters either attach directly to your faucet or connect via a hose and diverter valve. When the diverter is switched to the filtration setting, tap water filters through the unit on demand and into your glass, bottle, or pot. When the diverter is off, water flows straight out of the tap as normal.

Industry observers note that two major things to consider regarding faucet-connected systems are faucet compatibility and installation. Most aren’t compatible with pull-down, pull-out, spray, sensor-operated, or nonstandard faucets, and many also have small hoses that connect the faucet to the machine, which takes up a bit of space and can look cluttered. Some allow you to run the hoses from the machine to the plumbing under your sink, but that will require an adapter and a hole in the counter for the cords to route through.

While it can be tempting to choose the purification system for water that has the longest list of contaminants removed, it’s ultimately more notable to pair the system you choose with what you’re actually trying to filter out of your water.

Sources indicate that most of the best water filters have activated-carbon filters that remove unpleasant tastes and odors and may reduce other chemicals or particulates. Some systems add sediment filtration or specialty media to target things like lead, fluoride, or PFAS compounds. Since performance varies by model, always check the manufacturer’s claims rather than assuming they all work the same.

Reverse-osmosis systems use a membrane designed to reduce dissolved solids, which means they generally remove more contaminants than basic filtration systems. However, they can also reduce beneficial minerals, which is why some manufacturers are now adding a remineralization stage to return the filtered water to a more alkaline state.

Industry observers note that many of the units on this list carry third-party certification to verify tested performance beyond manufacturer claims. NSF International’s drinking-water treatment standards are the most commonly used, although you may also see mentions of accredited organizations like IAPMO R&T or WQA. While our tests using the Varify Complete Drinking Water Test Kit for this guide backed up the manufacturers’ claims, it’s still a good idea to prioritize products that carry filter certifications and look up which contaminants the product is certified to remove.

Then, match the certification to your specific concern. For example, if lead reduction is your main goal, you’ll want a model with NSF 53 and 58 listings.

According to recent reports, capacity has two meanings: how much water a filter can treat before replacement and how much filtered water the unit can provide at once. For our purposes, we’re defining it as how much it can filter at once, as we discuss filter life in the next section.

Since reservoir models’ ready-to-drink supply is based on the size of their clean-water chambers, larger households or those with greater needs will want to prioritize a model that holds multiple liters or gallons. Faucet-connected models can also be a good choice in those situations, as they can deliver clean water continuously as long as the tap is on.

Flow rate—how quickly the filter provides clean drinking water—is another key consideration. However, many manufacturers don’t list this information, and it can also vary depending on water pressure, source-water quality, temperature, and cartridge age. If this is a major concern, you may want to reach out to manufacturers directly or read online reviews for mentions of filtration speed.

In a recent development, every countertop drinking water filter system requires filter replacement on a set schedule, which means the true cost of ownership ends up being more than what you paid for it. When choosing between systems, compare the number of filters, their individual projected filter capacity, and each one’s replacement cost.

According to recent reports, A basic pitcher may use a single cartridge that’s easy to change but needs more frequent replacement, while a multistage RO unit may have multiple filters that each have different change intervals and prices. While systems with filter-life indicators can make it much easier to know when it’s time to swap them, if your unit is noticeably slower or isn’t providing the same quality, you may still need to change filters even if it isn’t technically time.

Countertop water filters are generally pretty straightforward, but the following answers to commonly asked questions can answer any lingering queries you may have.

According to recent reports, water filters work by using a filtration mechanism to capture organisms and chemicals that lead to unsafe or cloudy water. A fabricated surface traps the larger contaminants, while a compound like activated carbon works as a magnet to trap smaller contaminants.

Installation depends on the type: A faucet-connected filtration system typically attaches to a compatible faucet aerator or diverter valve, while dispenser, pitcher, gravity-fed, and countertop RO models generally only require rinsing the parts, installing the filters, and filling the reservoir. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, especially for RO units that may also require an initial flush cycle.

No, countertop water purification filters do not work with every type of kitchen faucet. Specifically, more modern designs and detachable faucets with spray nozzles may be incompatible with faucet-connected countertop water filters.

Most filters can remove chlorine, fluoride, bacteria, and parasites. To know exactly which contaminants a specific filter can remove or reduce, consult the manufacturer’s information regarding filter certification.

Yes, bacteria can grow in a countertop filter, so it’s a good idea to flush the faucet for about 20 seconds after turning on the water and then for an additional 5 to 10 seconds to filter and flush out any bacteria that may be lingering in the faucet.

Yes, countertop reverse osmosis systems are worth it for households seeking to remove dissolved contaminants like lead and fluoride and who prefer a plumbing-free setup. However, they generally cost more and require more maintenance than pitchers or carbon-filter-only units, so they’re best when your water test or local report identifies concerns simpler filters can’t address.

Industry observers note that filter replacement timing varies by system and filter type, so it’s best to follow the manufacturer’s schedule for your specific system. Generally speaking, pitcher and faucet units may need new filters every few months, while countertop RO filters and membranes may last anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. You may need to replace filters sooner if the flow slows noticeably or your water develops an unusual taste or odor.

Because she’d rather spend a little more up front than buy a tool or appliance twice, she strongly believes in the power of testing for finding quality items that are meant to last.

It has been revealed that my forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these issues, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of newly introduced legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

I recently covered related complications in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

According to recent reports, I’ve tested a lot of air purifiers, and most look like appliances I’d rather tuck out of sight in a corner. The Dupray Bloom Air Purifier is different. It combines a HEPA air purifier with a removable planter, turning something purely functional into a decorative accent. I planted a small fiddle-leaf fig in mine, and I love how it looks in the room. But I also wanted to know whether the Bloom’s unusual design would interfere with its primary job of filtering the air.

Absolutely, and that’s what makes the Bloom so appealing. The top features a removable planting pot with a root tray that helps keep roots above excess water. I chose a small fiddle-leaf fig, and once it was planted, the Bloom looked more like a decorative planter than an air-cleaning appliance.

It has been revealed that there is one thing I’d caution buyers about: The planter doesn’t have drainage holes. The root tray provides some separation from standing water, but it isn’t a substitute for proper watering. I’d recommend using an olla, a small porous automatic watering vessel that slowly releases moisture into the soil. It’s a good option for keeping the plant watered without repeatedly pouring water into a pot that can’t drain.

It has been revealed that I also appreciated that the planter lifts completely out. That means I can move the plant for maintenance or repotting without having to move the entire purifier. And when it’s time to replace the round HEPA filter, I can remove the planter, turn the unit over, and access the filter from the bottom.

Behind its decorative design, the Bloom is a serious air purifier. It uses an H13 HEPA filter with activated carbon to capture airborne particles, including dust, pollen, and pet dander, while helping reduce odors. Dupray rates it as capable of capturing 99.97 percent of particles as small as 0.1 micron.

Sources indicate that one feature I particularly liked was the stretchy fabric prefilter. It slips snugly over the purifier’s base, creating a smooth, modern appearance while catching larger airborne particles before they reach the HEPA filter. It’s washable, too, and Dupray offers replacement prefilters in different colors.

The Bloom also has an AutoDetect mode that monitors air quality and adjusts the fan speed. There are three manual fan settings, along with a sleep mode for quieter operation. Dupray rates its lowest noise level at just 24 decibels, making it suitable for bedrooms and other living spaces where a loud fan would be distracting.

It’s remarkably simple. The removable planter makes the HEPA filter accessible, and the fabric prefilter stretches on and off without clips or complicated fasteners.

Another smart touch is the universal power adapter. It comes with interchangeable plug configurations for the U.S., U.K., and Europe. That’s not something I typically see included with an air purifier.

It has been revealed that my only complaint—and it’s minor—is the digital control display. The symbols for Auto, Sleep, and the fan-speed bars looked slightly blurry to me. I could still identify them and operate the purifier, but a sharper display would have been easier to read. Or I might need a upcoming prescription for glasses.

In a recent development, at $249.99, the Bloom isn’t the cheapest way to get HEPA filtration, but its design sets it apart from the usual boxy models. It’s particularly appealing for living rooms, bedrooms, and home offices where an ordinary air purifier might detract from the decor.

Sources indicate that dupray advertises coverage up to 1,517 square feet, but that’s based on just one air change per hour. For more frequent air cleaning, it’s rated to cover 316 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. I’d use that smaller figure when choosing where to place it.

The Bloom also offers an optional wood tabletop model for anyone who prefers an accent table instead of a planter.

I love having a living plant incorporated into an appliance I’d otherwise try to hide. The Bloom is one of the few air purifiers I’ve tested that I’d happily put on display.

At $2,395 for the king size I tested, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper is absolutely a luxury purchase. After sleeping on it for 2 months during a Florida summer, however, I can say that its temperature-control technology delivers. This 2-inch topper uses fans, airflow, heating elements, and temperature sensors to regulate each side of the bed independently, creating a surprisingly effective way to stay comfortable throughout the night. While some aspects of the design could use a little more refinement, the actual cooling performance left me impressed.

Recent findings suggest that installation was straightforward. I unpacked the vacuum-sealed topper, laid it over my king mattress, added my usual fitted sheet, and plugged it in. The power supply is fairly significant, but I had no trouble tucking it down behind my headboard. The cables emerge from the head of the topper, which is worth keeping in mind if you tend to stretch your arms overhead while sleeping. As for comfort, the topper has an unusual feel at first—slightly firm but with enough give to stay comfortable. Its internal mesh structure allows air to circulate beneath you, and the effect is immediately noticeable, even on lower settings.

The cooling performance is easily my favorite feature. Even at level 3, I could feel a gentle, pleasant stream of cool air underneath me, which was especially welcome during warm Florida nights. The one trade-off is fan noise, which becomes quite noticeable at higher settings. Anything above level 5 was too loud for my sleeping preferences, but I found an easy workaround using the app’s scheduling feature. I’d run the cooling at a higher setting for about an hour before bedtime, then lower it to level 3 when I climbed into bed. This gave me the best of both worlds: a wonderfully cool mattress at bedtime and gentle, nearly silent cooling throughout the night.

There are a few areas where I’d love to see Perfectly Snug make improvements, especially considering the premium price. The power supply and small side-mounted control panel are functional but have a fairly basic appearance. I also occasionally brushed against the fans positioned at the foot of the topper, which could briefly interrupt their operation (making a noticeable “you’ve just stopped a fan from moving” type of buzzing sound). The companion app was another underwhelming aspect of the experience. While it offers useful features like scheduling and temperature adjustments, its interface feels super dated and could benefit from a much more polished, intuitive design. None of these concerns prevented me from enjoying the topper, but they’re details I’d expect to see addressed at this price point.

Ultimately, the Perfectly Snug Smart Topper gets the most key thing right: keeping your bed at a comfortable temperature. I enjoyed slipping into a perfectly cooled bed each night, and the subtle airflow on lower settings noticeably improved my sleep comfort. It’s an innovative product with plenty to offer, particularly for hot sleepers or couples with different temperature preferences. Although the fan noise and a few less-refined design elements keep it from feeling like a truly premium experience, the core technology is admirable. With some thoughtful improvements, this could be an outstanding luxury sleep upgrade.

Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (439 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.
  • [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met.
  • It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing fresh terms for future cooperation in any event….
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.

[W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed new limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing fresh terms for future cooperation in any event….

[But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a latest state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "problem orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

According to recent reports, we also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

The Best Leaf Vacuums for Clearing Fall Leaves

Whether you bag your fallen leaves for curbside disposal or reuse them in your yard and garden, a leaf vacuum makes lawn care more efficient. According to Brad Saunders, president of Heroes Lawn Care, “A leaf vacuum is all about convenience. If you’re tired of raking up leaves or constantly bending over to gather them after using a leaf blower, a leaf vacuum could be a solution.” Vacuums collect, grind, and bag leaves, seeds, and debris for easy disposal or composting. Our Product Reviews team has researched dozens of leaf vacuums and tested 14 of them in our search for the best models for home use.

Recent findings suggest that our top pick is the Toro Ultra Electric Leaf Blower Vacuum. It blows, vacuums, and mulches, plus it’s lightweight and powerful to boot. But being tied to a power cord, it may not be as well suited for larger properties as others on the list. Read on for our reviews of this model and others that we consider the best leaf vacuums for yards of all sizes, and the most important considerations to bear in mind while shopping.

Industry observers note that we narrowed the field of the best leaf vacuum for yard​ work by testing several popular models in different categories, with the performance results in the reviews below. Keeping the yard, garage, and flower beds free of fallen leaves can be easier with any of these top picks.

In a recent development, the Toro Ultra leaf vacuum mulcher is a powerful three-in-one leaf blower, high-speed vacuum, and leaf shredder designed for midsize yards. The 12A electric motor moves up to 340 CFM of air at speeds as high as 260 mph. In vacuum mode, the impeller leaf vacuum shredder grinds to a 16:1 ratio, with 97 percent of shredded debris measuring less than ½ inch in diameter.

Recent findings suggest that in our tests, this plug-in leaf blower with vacuum had no trouble handling loads of leaves—no clogs and only slight hesitation in heavier piles. Moist leaves moved a bit more slowly but were sucked up and ground nonetheless. The compact, lightweight body of this blower vacuum was easy to maneuver, and the vacuum mulcher output was comparable to the others we tested.

In addition to its outdoor vacuum capabilities, this variable-speed unit was just as effective at keeping grass clippings off the driveway and banishing dust and debris from between potted patio plants as it was at clearing fallen leaves. The unique dispersion nozzle blower attachment focused air in a low, wide pattern that reduced dust clouds, but the narrow blow tube makes the going slower than some of the other models we tested which will matter most for larger yards.

According to recent reports, what our tester says: “No need to buy an expensive battery tool for a chore you only do once or twice a year. The Toro Ultra Leaf Blower/Vacuum does a fantastic job picking up and mulching leaves and debris for disposal at a fraction of the cost of cordless, and offers unlimited runtime.” –Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews writer and tester.

Get the Toro leaf vacuum at Lowe’s, Tractor Supply Co, or Ace Hardware.

Battery tools cost more than corded electric models and require charging, but they also offer freedom of movement without the noise and fumes of a gas engine. The LV5000 56V 3-in-1 leaf leaf blower vacuum combo from Ego Power+ provides the power and runtime needed for routine yard maintenance and seasonal leaf cleanup in midsize yards. Those who already own Ego Power+ battery tools can purchase the bare LV5000 for a significant discount compared to the kit with battery and charger.

Industry observers note that after an hour blowing and vacuum mulching with this unit, we were most impressed by its operating speed and durable build quality. Reconfiguring from blower to vacuum mode was a quick, straightforward process of swapping the blow tube for the collection bag and installing the suction tube at the opposite end. It took less than a minute thanks to the quick connection system. We had no trouble doing it without removing our work gloves. The 16:1 mulching ratio was about average for the group, but this unit packed its collection bag tighter than most, which allowed it to collect more per load.

In a recent development, the common complaint about multi-task tools not being optimized for every task holds true with this one. While the unit excelled in vacuum/mulcher mode, as a leaf blower it is a bit heavier than similarly powered dedicated handheld models. To us, the small tradeoff in weight is worth the space and budget savings of owning a single machine.

What our tester states: “Ego Power+ continues to impress with power to spare and a good runtime per charge. This new 2026 introduction does not reset the market with technological upgrades, but it does include refinements to the attachment system monitoring screen that give it a leg up on older models.” –Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Ego Power+ leaf vacuum at Amazon (tool only) or Acme Tools.

In a recent development, the Worx WG509 boasts yard-clearing convenience at a budget-friendly price. It changes between its three modes with the flip of a switch; there’s no need to change the tube or use tools to go from blowing to vacuuming. In mulcher mode, a metal impeller reduces leaves in an 18:1 ratio (18 bags to 1 bag). The 1-bushel collection bag includes a shoulder strap to reduce fatigue.

This leaf blower/vac proved to have one of the best designs of any model, at any price. It is the only unit we tested that can change from blower to vacuum without completely reconfiguring the tubes, which made it super easy to work with. It also delivered power comparable to models costing twice as much. It did clog on some coarse debris, but it performed well overall.

The model only has two speeds, but it reaches a top speed of 210 mph with 350 CFM. An ergonomic tube design reduces back strain by putting the tube at a parallel angle to the ground. The angle also helps it reach under and around landscaping elements.

Get the Worx leaf vacuum at Amazon, Target, Best Buy, or Worx.

Industry observers note that if you already own a leaf blower, then a dedicated leaf vacuum might be all you need. The Ryobi 40V HP leaf vacuum is one of the best single-purpose mulching leaf vacuums we’ve tested. It has strong suction to pick up loads of wet and dry leaves, and grinds them to a 16:1 mulching ratio, minimizing volume in the collection bag.

Industry observers note that the included 40-volt 6-amp-hour battery works with dozens of different Ryobi tools, including some of the brand’s most powerful yard equipment. In our test, it charged from zero to full in about an hour, and ran for a little more than 30 minutes per charge.

Industry observers note that this unit was more user-friendly than many of the dual-purpose leaf blower/vacuums we tested. With the collection bag attached, it was well balanced and easy to maneuver back and forth to pick up leaves, and we especially liked the bag closure system. Instead of a zipper, it is equipped with heavy-duty plastic buckles that are easy to operate with gloved hands. Emptying the bag only takes a few seconds because there is no constriction point—the opening is the full width of the bag.

Get the Ryobi leaf vacuum at The Home Depot.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a budget-priced combination leaf vacuum, mulcher, and blower and don’t mind the limitations that come with a cord, then this model from Craftsman is worth considering. It’s one of the most powerful corded models we’ve seen, with a max air volume of 450 CFM and air speed of 260 mph. While it won’t rival the more powerful gas models we tested, it has enough vacuuming muscle to gather a moderate covering of leaves on a small area. After testing its blowing capability, we converted it to a leaf vacuum, a process that takes only a minute or two.

It produces enough power to suck up small piles of leaves quickly and shreds them into fine pieces that fit into a large 55-liter bag. Unlike other handhelds that use a single strap, the Craftsman has a two-strap backpack-style collection bag that’s more ergonomic and hence more comfortable to wear. Even carrying a full load of damp shredded leaves was surprisingly comfortable.

It has been revealed that while the Craftsman is one of the cheapest leaf vacuums out there with a price tag of around $100, there are some compromises with this model. With its corded design and middle-of-the-road power, this backpack leaf vacuum is best suited for collecting leaves in smaller yards and in and around landscaping, decks, and porches.

Get the Craftsman leaf vacuum at Amazon or Lowe’s.

Industry observers note that for large gardens and heavy leaf accumulation, it’s hard to beat the Husqvarna gas leaf blower vacuum, which draws in air at speeds of up to 170 mph and features an air volume of 425 CFM. Its easy-crank engine enables quick starting, and an auto-return stop switch automatically resets the vacuum for simpler starting. It also features cruise control for easier handling and less hand fatigue.

After fueling up with a 50:1 mix of gasoline to 2-cycle oil, the Husqvarna engine started easily with just two pulls. Powerful air movement at the suction tube easily pulled in piles of leaves, and the tube remained unclogged, even when pulling in wet debris. The mulching knives aggressively shredded twigs as well as leaves without a problem. The only glitch we experienced was the slightly awkward feel of the curved tube that feeds the bag with shredded leaves.

Though the unit weighs in at 9.6 pounds, a shoulder strap helps support the vacuum to reduce arm fatigue. The Husqvarna also features anti-vibration technology to reduce hand stress.

Get the Husqvarna leaf vacuum at Amazon.

Leave the leaves? Mulch them into the lawn? Bag and remove? The Greenworks Pro 80V Mower with Turbo Leaf Pickup gives you the most options. As a lawnmower, it provides ample runtime for yards up to a half acre, and excellent airflow for bagging clippings. At the push of a button, Turbo Leaf Pickup mode increases motor output for fine shredding and bagging.

Our test lawn had significant overlap of mowing season and leaf season conditions, so we appreciated the ability to cover both tasks at once. Until the leaves began to fall heavily, we simply mulched them into the lawn. No need to use the bagger until the grass growth slowed and leaf drop increased. In turbo leaf pickup mode, the Greenworks Pro 80V mower did a really nice job packing debris all the way to the back of the collection bag.

This could be the best option for those with limited storage space. Just keep in mind that it may not completely eliminate the need for raking or blowing, especially around landscape beds, patios, and other non-mowable areas where leaves might accumulate.

Get the Greenworks lawn mower leaf vacuum at Amazon, Lowe’s, Greenworks, or Walmart (with 8 Ah battery).

Sources indicate that for larger properties with lots of trees and a mix of grassy and hard surfaces to maintain, a walk-behind leaf vacuum could be the best machine for the job. The Billy Goat KV601SP is a small commercial leaf vacuum that is also a good option for large private properties. It features a wide nozzle with powerful suction and an oversize bagger to clean large areas swiftly with less downtime for emptying.

Industry observers note that this walk-behind commercial leaf vacuum with bag​ attached comes equipped with a 190cc Briggs & Stratton gas engine that delivers a whopping 1,707 CFM of airflow through the 26-inch nozzle and powers the rear drive wheels. A serrated impeller grinds dry leaves and debris at a 12:1 reduction ratio before sending it to the 4-bushel bagger. The heavy-duty zipperless bagger uses a clip closure for fast debris removal.

Sources indicate that this machine includes an adjustable-height nozzle to capture different types of debris, including leaves and pine needles, pine cones, acorns, flower petals, and more. It works well on a variety of surfaces, such as grass, gravel, mulch, and pavement. An optional hose kit (sold separately) expands the vacuum’s functionality to include debris that lands on hedges, between shrubs, and in other hard-to-reach areas.

In a recent development, our walk-behind leaf vacuum test included a heavy layer of leaves, clumpy grass clippings, twigs, pine needles, and pine cones on grass and concrete. The Billy Goat rolled along and picked up everything in its path. Matted wet foliage sometimes required a second pass, and longer sticks partly blocked the nozzle a couple of times, but the impeller never became clogged and the bagger held an impressive amount of material.

Sources indicate that in the absence of a blower to remove litter from hard-to-reach spots, we would have appreciated the hose attachment to access these pesky areas. Still, this was far and away the fastest and most thorough tool for the job.

Get the Billy Goat leaf vacuum at Acme Tools or Mowers at Jacks.

We set up a leafy obstacle course and tested each of these tools for at least an hour. We wanted to see how well they piled leaves (if applicable), and how they reduced leaf piles for disposal or reuse in the yard. The debris included freshly fallen leaves as well as old, built-up debris that had accumulated beneath shrubs over the course of a year.

According to recent reports, throughout the process, we recorded our observations on a scoring rubric. We tracked measurables such as tool weight, charge time, run time, and how quickly a vacuum loaded its collection bag without clogging. We also noted subjective observations regarding operating comfort, ease of use, and perceived value. Finally, we used the scoring rubric to assign award titles.

Industry observers note that leaf vacuums come in various types and with different-size collection bags. There are also three power source types—gas, electric, and cordless/battery—with each option affecting runtime and suction. Take a look below at some crucial factors to help determine the motor type, power, and design that will work best for you.

Leaf vacuums are made in a few types, and some kinds work better in certain situations and setups than others.

Like lawn mowers, leaf vacuums are available in electric- and gas-powered versions.

It has been revealed that to figure out the power of a leaf vacuum, check the product description for two numbers: mph and CFM. The mph stands for miles per hour—in this case, referring to how swiftly air is suctioned into the unit and through the tube. Most units run between 110 and 180 mph, although some may reach extremes of 250 mph or so.

Industry observers note that somewhat more important than airspeed, however, is CFM. This describes how much air moves through the vacuum in the span of 60 seconds, indicating how powerful the unit is. While mph provides an idea of how quickly leaves can go through the tube, CFM indicates how much can go through all at once.

The CFM rankings for leaf vacuums range between 150 to 600. A unit with a CFM under 200 may be all that’s needed to clean up an apartment balcony or a small yard, but for larger areas, it may be desirable to invest in a unit with higher CFM.

Saunders recommends a leaf vacuum with a strong motor “that can really get the job done.” He adds, “Something like a 12-amp electric motor, which you’ll find in some top models, will give you the suction power you need to handle a good amount of leaves without getting bogged down.”.

The runtime of a battery-powered leaf vacuum can limit the amount of work that can be done. Most models offer at least 20 to 30 minutes of runtime on the highest power levels. At lower levels, the battery may run for 45 minutes or more.

In a recent development, battery-powered models that include two or more interchangeable batteries can increase the available work time. While one battery is in use, the other battery charges. Charge times vary from 1.5 to 3 hours and sometimes longer depending on the battery size. The amount of work may still be limited with interchangeable batteries, but it will provide more work time than a single battery.

Some manufacturers provide batteries that are interchangeable with the brand’s other power tools. In these cases, buying power tools of the same brand can add to the number of batteries available. Ultimately, that can extend possible work time even more.

According to recent reports, some leaf vacuums offer bells and whistles beyond simple suction. In fact, most vacuums these days are actually leaf blowers with a vacuum function. That provides extra use options with a single tool.

Recent findings suggest that leaf vacuums are best suited for smaller outdoor spaces, like those surrounding garden apartments and duplexes. Some models also offer a mulching option, which is great for repurposing leaves into healthy plant beds.

A leaf vacuum’s mix of features and design can make it easier or harder to use. Bag size, for example, determines how often it will need to be emptied. Larger bags mean less frequent emptying, but they can be awkward and heavy to carry.

Weight also affects ease of use. Gas-powered leaf vacuums weigh the most, though some battery-powered models are almost as heavy. For those with a large yard, gas power makes sense because it can keep a consistent high power throughout the whole yard.

According to recent reports, however, for those with smaller yards, the lightweight nature of a handheld or a battery-powered model can be more comfortable. Models with a backpack bag combine the lighter weight of a handheld leaf vacuum with the convenience of a backpack.

Ergonomics is also something to take into consideration. “You’re going to be using this tool for a while, so it needs to be comfortable,” Saunders states. “Lightweight models are easier on the arms and back, especially if you’re working in a large yard. Features like an ergonomically designed tube can also make a substantial difference by reducing strain.”.

Finally, there are controls to consider. Trigger switches and on/off buttons directly on the handle are easier to use. This allows you to turn the machine on or off with one hand. Toolless conversion for hybrid models can also add to ease of use.

Leaf vacuums aren’t complicated once you understand how they work and what features are needed for specific jobs. However, since they aren’t as common as leaf blowers, you might still find yourself scratching your head as you look at the specs. Here, we answer some of the most common questions about leaf vacuums to help you make the right choice.

Industry observers note that A leaf vacuum is the best machine for picking up leaves. Choose one that matches your yard size and typical leaf volume. Battery-powered handheld models work best for small yards with a moderate amount of leaves. Electric and gas models offer longer running times and a larger collection bag capacity for larger areas and heavier leaf cover.

It has been revealed that A leaf vacuum needs a minimum rating of 340 CFM and 150 mph to pick up dry material effectively. Leaf removal equipment rated above 500 CFM and 180 mph is best for large areas and wet leaves and debris.

Yes, a lawn vacuum will effectively pick up dry and clumped grass clippings.

No, leaf vacuums are not designed to clean gutters. They don’t offer the required suction or reach to do the job.

Recent findings suggest that to switch a dual-purpose leaf blower/vac from blower to vacuum mode, remove the blower tube and intake guard; then attach the vacuum tube (to the air intake) and the collection bag (where the blower tube came off). Check the owner’s manual for specific instructions.

Yes, leaf vacuums can be noisy, especially those with gas engines. Some models can reach 90 decibels. However, those powered by rechargeable batteries are much quieter, in the 60 to 80 decibel range.

Recent findings suggest that to clean an outdoor vacuum for leaves, first turn it off and disconnect the power cord or battery. Empty the collection bag, including anything that may not easily dump out. Remove and unclog the suction nozzle, and clear any debris from the impeller.

Leaf vacuums will last 8 to 10 years or longer with routine maintenance.

Leaf vacuum prices range from about $100 to more than $1000, depending on the design and size.

Mark Wolfe is a writer and product tester with a background in the nursery and landscaping industry. For more than 20 years he mowed, edged, planted, pruned, cultivated, irrigated, and renovated beautiful landscapes. Now he tests and writes reviews about the latest outdoor power equipment, hand tools, lawn care products, and other outdoor living goods.

#227856. Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (725 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement.
  • Sources indicate that we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements.
  • Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's new law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:.

Sources indicate that we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.

We conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. Latest Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

Sources indicate that the anti-mask law presents more difficult complications because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:.

It has been revealed that at bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law. Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’ve tested several Aiper cleaners over the years, and the Aiper Scuba V3 Ultra feels like a natural evolution of the brand’s previous models. I ran it through repeated cleaning cycles in my 8,500-gallon saltwater pool in Florida, where leaves, bugs, fine debris, and the occasional patch of algae give pool robots plenty to deal with. Setup was super simple: The Aiper app connected quickly, the robot updated without any fuss, and I had it in the water about 15 minutes after opening the box.

Sources indicate that what impressed me right away was just how much the Scuba V3 Ultra can do in one cleaning cycle. Plenty of the robotic pool cleaners we’ve tested at Bob Vila handle floors, walls, and the waterline, but only a select few can also skim floating debris from the surface. That matters in my open-air pool, which regularly collects bugs and leaves. Anything the Aiper actually reaches gets cleaned extremely well.

Recent findings suggest that the MicroMesh filter is another highlight. It traps extremely fine material, including algae and sediment that can slip through coarser filter baskets. Cleaning that ultra-fine layer takes a little more effort—I usually spend a few minutes thoroughly rinsing it with a hose and then leave it out to dry—but that’s a fair trade-off for how much fine material it captures. The app is also among the better pool-cleaner apps I’ve used, and I like getting a notification when the cleaning cycle is finished. The robot then floats neatly near the pool edge for retrieval.

Sources indicate that where the V3 Ultra disappointed me was its claim of shallow-area cleaning. Aiper says it can work in water down to about 7.9 inches deep, but my sun shelf is apparently too shallow for it to clean reliably. I still have to brush debris from the shelf into the main pool and let the robot collect it there. It also won’t clean my pool steps. For a $2,300 machine marketed around near-total pool coverage, those are significant omissions—especially since sun shelves have become so common in newer pools.

Still, I’m a fan of the Scuba V3 Ultra overall. My older Aiper cleaner has been running reliably for close to two years, which gives me more confidence in the brand than I’d have from a short-term test alone. The voice assistant is useful without being obnoxious, retrieval is simple, filtration is excellent, and cleaning performance everywhere the robot can reach is phenomenal. I’m still waiting for the robot that will truly clean every inch of my pool, but the Scuba V3 Ultra gets closer than most.

If maintained properly—and that means having the right tool—wood flooring can hold its finish for years without damage or cracking. Some brooms, for instance, can be too abrasive, whereas mops designed to clean hardwood floors are ideal for these surfaces.

In a recent development, it can be tricky to pick a floor mop that suits your cleaning style and budget, as well as the degree of dirt and stains on your flooring. To help you find the best mop for your situation, we put a host of different products through their paces in a home with plenty of dust, dirt, and pet hair. We also spoke to professionals like Ryan Knoll, owner of Tidy Casa in Scottsdale, Arizona, to get a bit of expert knowledge on what shoppers will want to look for in a mop. Read on to see what to look for in the best mops for wood floors, as well as our reviews of products we deem superior in today’s crowded market.

Bottom line: Discover the best mops for wood floors, tested for performance and ease of use, to keep your hardwood looking pristine.

Many do not know what to look for in the best mops for hardwood floors, but here are some real-life reviews to get you started. The very wide rectangular mophead with a 360-degree swivel action meant less work on large hardwood floors, since with fewer swipes and greater maneuverability, we got our dusting and wet-mopping jobs done quickly.

At first, we were stumped on how to moisten the cleaning cloth, but a bit of online research taught us a few tricks for microfiber mops. Simply wet the cloth, roll it up to wring it out, then attach it to the mophead base. The microfiber mop cloths are reusable—just toss in the washing machine to launder. A handy dirt scrubber attachment is included for tight corners and tough grime, and the mop can be used on a variety of surfaces, including marble, tile, and laminate, as well as hardwood.

According to recent reports, the O-Cedar ProMist Max Microfiber Spray Mop seemed promising with its unique wraparound flat mophead (akin to a mitten on the base of the mop). But in practice, it absorbed liquid (including its own cleaning fluid) poorly, and merely smeared dirt and dried ketchup around. We wanted to like its lightweight design, but it felt cheap and flimsy, particularly the trigger-spray handle.

We put a series of mops for hardwood floors, both cordless and corded, through their paces in a typical home that accumulated dust, dirt, pet hair, and muddy paw prints. We used the mops with their provided cleaners or distilled water, as recommended by the manufacturers.

According to recent reports, we noted how easy or difficult the mops were to assemble, and considered the practicality of storing them. Finally, we used each in a controlled test of dried mud and ketchup smeared on hardwood floors and noted how much mess each floor mop left behind.

In a recent development, when purchasing a mop for wood flooring, think about its ease of use, any cleaning solutions it dispenses, and the price. In addition to the tool itself, factor in the size of the area that needs mopping. Here are some notable considerations to look at when looking at mops for wood floors.

There are different types of mops available to suit various floor-maintenance preferences: flat mops, string mops, steam mops, and dust mops. Some are used exclusively for dusting floors, while other kinds function as both wet and dry mops.

According to recent reports, old-fashioned dunk-in-a-bucket mops require hand-wringing, but there are more convenient, less-messy options today. These mops may feature electric or mechanical components for wringing, as well as either reusable or disposable parts, so look for the type and system that suits your cleaning preference, floor type, and floor size.

The business end of a floor mop is typically either disposable or reusable. Disposable options are convenient for quick touch-ups and smaller floors, while reusable ones often prove more budget-friendly and can tackle larger surfaces.

According to recent reports, both types of mopheads impact sustainability, but in different ways. Reusable mopheads require water and chemicals to launder after use, while disposable versions head straight to the landfill. For larger areas, a reusable, machine-washable mophead is probably more efficient and eco-friendly than using multiple disposable mopheads per cleaning session. Those who prefer a reusable option might consider microfiber mopheads, which will catch and hold dirt and liquids better than materials such as cotton or sponge while reducing the look of scratches and scuffs.

Industry observers note that according to Knoll, “Microfiber is the go-to. It’s soft, absorbent, and won’t damage your floors. It also wrings out well, keeping the water usage minimal.” He also added that microfiber mops are “great for picking up dust and fine particles without leaving scratches.”.

If pushing a manual mop around seems laborious and inefficient, consider an electric model. These products typically have a variety of cleaning modes and processes (including one specifically for wood floors), and may feature the use of steam and/or cleaning solutions. They often come with swiveling heads for easier maneuverability, too.

Recent findings suggest that electric mops may be corded or cordless—and both types require access to an outlet. Corded mops must be plugged in during use, while the battery charger of cordless models must be plugged in as well. The portability of cordless models tends to appeal to folks who don’t want to be tied down to the length of a cord, typically because they have large areas to clean, and sometimes on different levels.

It has been revealed that when stubborn dirt and stains occur, wood floors may require more vigorous cleaning than just dry-mopping, but only with a product specifically formulated for hardwood flooring. While hardwood floors are usually finished and sealed, some versions may be unsealed—it’s important to avoid using water on unsealed hardwood floors, as well as harsh cleansers on any wood floor. An all-purpose floor cleaner, for instance, may dull or, worse, strip the finish.

According to recent reports, though there are different types of cleaning solutions, those that can be used straight from the container without diluting tend to be safer, since any excess water from mixing a concentrated formula can seep into the wood and damage it. Some mops employ steam to clean and sanitize flooring, which should be safe for sealed hardwood—but to be safe, consult and follow all directions to avoid damage.

Knoll recommends gentle cleaners: “Opt for pH-neutral, hardwood-specific cleaners to prevent damage.” Also, “damp mopping is the way. Ensure the mop is just moist enough to clean without leaving excess water.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to mopping around furniture, under beds/sofas, and into hard-to-reach areas, maneuverability matters. A swivel-head mop is ideal for getting around obstacles. The shape of the mophead (circular, triangular, or rectangular) also impacts how easily it can access corners and tight spots.

In a recent development, mops may also include ergonomic features, some of which affect maneuvering, like telescoping handles to adjust length, and thereby extend reach. A poorly designed handle can also lead to arm and hand fatigue, so customers will want to look for a model with a grip that feels good.

Those who still want more information on cleaning hardwood flooring with a quality mop may find it here in the answers to some of the most common questions about this household chore.

Industry observers note that mopping correctly can be a great way to maintain hardwood flooring, but using the wrong cleaning products can actually damage these expensive surfaces. A damp mop is often all that’s required to clean a hardwood floor; if the mop is too wet (with water or cleaning solution), excess liquid can seep into the cracks, causing the wood to warp.

Industry observers note that cleaning a floor starts with removing dust and debris by sweeping, vacuuming, or dry-mopping. For stubborn dirt and stains, use a cleaner designed for the specific floor material, using a “less is more” approach according to the manufacturer’s directions. To mop a floor correctly, dip string or sponge mops in the cleaning fluid, wring it out, and then swab with the damp mop. Use plain water to do a final rinse if desired. Start mopping in a far corner of the room, moving in the direction of the grain on hardwood floors, and work your way to the door. When finished, rinse the mop and let it air dry or wash any reusable pads.

Swiffer’s heavy-duty pads are considered safe for linoleum, vinyl, laminate, and ceramic tile, as well as sealed wood, marble, and stone. They should not be used on unsealed wood floors. As with all floor cleaners, be cautious using any fluid on unfinished, damaged, or especially delicate materials.

The National Wood Flooring Association recommends a heavy-duty mopping on wood floors monthly with a wood-flooring cleaner. However, it is safe to dry-mop daily or do a light mop on high-traffic areas once a week. For those without children and pets, feel free to give a very light mop on light-traffic areas more often.

#227847. Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (791 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

Second Amendment Roundup, I: The Common Use Test and the Federal "Assault Weapon" Ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v.
  • That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.
  • First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, connecticut argues before the Supreme Court, in its Grant v. Higgins brief, that before 2004, "few civilians owned AR-15s." That was supposedly "because federal law prohibited 'manufacture, transfer, or possess[ion]' of the weapons between 1994 and 2004" under Pub. L. No. 103-322, 108 Stat. 1796, 1996-97 (1994). That was the federal "assault weapon ban" that expired in 2004. The brief continues, "Under the common-use-only approach, if Congress had extended that legislation in 2004, AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today.".

That argument exhibits a profoundly mistaken view about the what the federal law actually did.

First, while the law made it "unlawful for a person to manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon," that provision did "not apply to the possession or transfer of any semiautomatic assault weapon otherwise lawfully possessed under Federal law on the date of the enactment of this subsection."  18 U.S.C. § 922(v). So it did not ban possession or transfer of a single firearm that was already lawfully possessed. Moreover, the federal law did not ban future manufacture of the subject firearms as long as certain aspects were eliminated. The firearms were defined, first, in a list of names, including "Colt AR-15" and "copies or duplicates" thereof. Second, they included certain features, including:.

a semiautomatic rifle that has an ability to accept a detachable magazine and has at least 2 of –.

(i) a folding or telescoping stock;.

(ii) a pistol grip that protrudes conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon;.

(iv) a flash suppressor or threaded barrel designed to accommodate a flash suppressor; and.

Sources indicate that (v) a grenade launcher…. 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(30).

Recent findings suggest that under the above, Colt could not engrave simply "AR-15" on its rifles, but could use other names. A manufacturer could not make a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, but as discussed below, a rifle would be a "copy or duplicate" of an AR-15, inter alia, only if it had at least two of the five listed features.

But guess what: the sine qua non of an AR-15 is the conspicuously protruding pistol grip. None of the other features listed above are inherent in the AR-15 design. Many AR-15s never had a folding or telescoping stock. How many people cared whether it had a bayonet mount? A flash suppressor (or threading "designed" to accommodate one) could not be mounted, but a muzzle brake or compensator could. Congress must have included grenade launcher to sound dramatic, as that was already restricted under the National Firearms Act.

And so the federal law did exactly nothing to "ban" the basic AR-15 design. Manufacturers kept making and consumers kept buying semiautomatic rifles with protruding pistol grips sans bayonet mounts.

It has been revealed that manufacturers submitted samples of rifles to the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to verify compliance. I have reproduced some samples of ATF approval letters in my Firearms Law Deskbook § 10:6 (available in book form or on Westlaw). As an example, ATF examined a Bushmaster XM-15E2, which was "based on the AR15 design and incorporates a pistol grip that extends conspicuously beneath the action of the weapon." However, it had none of the other listed features. It did have a muzzle brake, but it was not a flash suppressor. The rifle was found not to be an assault weapon "because it does not have at least two of the features specified in the statute. Additionally, the firearm is not a copy or duplicate of the Colt AR15 rifle." Edward M. Owen, Jr., Chief, ATF Firearms Technology Branch, Feb. 16, 1996.

Instead of a two-feature test like the expired federal law, Connecticut bans rifles based on a single feature, including: "Any grip of the weapon, including a pistol grip, a thumbhole stock, or any other stock, the use of which would allow an individual to grip the weapon, resulting in any finger on the trigger hand in addition to the trigger finger being directly below any portion of the action of the weapon when firing…." This is a more capacious ban that affects a much broader collection of firearms than the expired federal law.

Connecticut is wrong to argue that had Congress extended its law in 2004, "AR-15s would never have entered into common use—and thus could be banned today." AR-15s were already in common use in 1994. The fact is that the federal law did nothing to dampen the ever-increasing demand for and use by the American people of the AR-15 basic design. And it goes without saying that semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines had already been around for a century when the federal law was in place.

Sources indicate that police sirens can sound very different, from a slow wail to a rapid yelp. Here’s why officers switch tones and what drivers should do.

Recent findings suggest that everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Industry observers note that officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

In a recent development, different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:.

It has been revealed that modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

According to recent reports, officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

Sources indicate that A portable workbench should be lightweight and durable, and it should have the features to assist with a number of projects. After all, a portable workbench’s most desirable feature should be versatility. Keep the following considerations in mind while shopping for one of these tools.

In a recent development, when shopping for a portable workbench, size and weight are crucial. Most portable workbenches weigh less than 30 pounds, which is a manageable weight for one person. Some workbenches weigh as little as 15 pounds, though 25 to 30 pounds is the most typical weight range.

In a recent development, some portable workbenches fold flat to between 4 and 7 inches thick to allow for easy transport and storage. When set up, most portable workbenches have worktops that are approximately 30 inches long by 24 inches wide and stand about 30 inches off the ground, but this varies by model.

It has been revealed that portable workbenches should be sturdy enough to endure abuse but also light enough to transport. To achieve this balance, most workbenches are made of a combination of sturdy steel and lightweight ABS plastic or wood. Some portable workbenches feature steel or aluminum legs that provide a sturdy support system with a benchtop of heavy-duty plastic resin or a lighter wood such as bamboo.

In a recent development, when working on a project, a wobbly surface just won’t do, so a portable workbench must be sturdy. Portable workbenches feature wide-set feet with steel or aluminum legs that help provide stability. Look for a portable workbench with feet coated in rubber or some other nonslip material to prevent the bench from sliding.

Most portable workbenches feature integrated clamping systems. While some portable models have entire benchtops that open to clamp large material, others integrate tracks into the worktop to incorporate holding clamps and large 2-inch bar clamps. These clamps are designed to secure large pieces of wood or metal, allowing the user to cut, sand, or fasten materials.

Many portable workbenches include special features to make life easier. For example, some workbenches are designed with molded handles to make transport easier, whereas others may include measurement markings printed or molded onto the worktop surface. Still other models feature extra pockets and drawers for tool storage, while some even have integrated power strips.

Sources indicate that portable workbenches are designed to meet a variety of demands, and versatility is their greatest benefit. Some workbenches may double as workstations for miter saws, while others have the ability to change shape completely, allowing them to function as both a workbench and sawhorse.

Many workbenches allow users to change the worktop’s height by up to 4 inches, which is handy when using the workbench with a table saw or as a support for cutting longer material. Other styles allow users to change the angle of the workbench to use as a fence for cutting.

If you’re wondering which qualities to look for in a workbench, keep reading for some of the most frequently asked questions about the top portable workbenches.

A quality portable workbench should be durable enough to handle the rigors of a home workshop or pro job site. It should have a sturdy base that prevents it from wobbling while you work. It should include clamping features to hold materials securely in place. A portable workbench also should break down in seconds into a shape that’s compact and light enough for one person to manage.

In a recent development, unlike dining room tables or kitchen counters, no standard workbench height exists. Workbench heights can range from 28 inches to 38 inches. Workbench heights on the high end are suitable for assembling items and to function as outfeed tables for table saws, while lower workbench heights allow for more leverage for such jobs as sanding. If you’re not sure which height you need, use this literal rule of thumb—the benchtop should meet the same level as the knuckle in your thumb when standing with your arms hanging at your sides.

The weight capacity of workbenches varies. Lighter-duty workbenches can handle a weight of around 250 pounds, which is adequate for most home workshops, while a heavy-duty workbench may have a weight capacity as high as 1,000 pounds.

Most portable workbenches use plastic in their design. While this makes them much lighter than a permanent workbench, plastic isn’t as durable as wood or steel. Plus, portable workbenches have movable joints that allow them to collapse, making them weaker than a standard workbench with no moving parts. With that in mind, most portable workbenches should last many years when properly maintained.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

According to recent reports, the Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

It depends. Salting before a big storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

Blueprint to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

Sources indicate that it’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

It has been revealed that the best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, claims.

Apply salt before and after a major storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

According to recent reports, “Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, claims. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

According to recent reports, if only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

“The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how major the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski says. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland says. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

Rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski says. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

Recent findings suggest that yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski notes.

It has been revealed that there’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

Second Amendment Roundup, II: Much Ado About Bowie Knives
